title: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
summary: How OCR finds text (EAST, DBNet), reads it with CRNN and CTC, gets scored with CER and WER, and how layout-aware and OCR-free models such as LayoutLM and Donut turn pages into structured answers.
outcomes: Explain why OCR splits into text detection and sequence recognition, and how errors propagate to extracted fields
Decode a CTC output by merging repeats then dropping blanks, and explain why the blank enables double letters
Compute CER and WER from an edit-distance alignment and explain why normalization changes them
Build LayoutLM-style 0 to 1000 box inputs and contrast OCR-based models with OCR-free Donut
Compute ANLS for document QA answers and explain its 0.5 threshold

lessons.title: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it

blocks.md:
Optical character recognition (OCR) turns pixels that show text into a string. *Document understanding* goes one step further: it turns a page into structure, such as the fields of an invoice, the cells of a table, or the answer to a question about the page.

A receipt scanner needs both. OCR reads `TOTAL 125.00`; a structure step decides that 125.00 is the total and not the tax.

Why not just run the object detector from the previous course and classify each character? Three reasons.

- **Characters touch and vary.** Cursive, tight kerning and blur make single-character boxes ambiguous, so cutting a word into letters is itself error-prone.
- **Text has odd shapes.** Words and lines are long, thin, often rotated or curved, so a few axis-aligned anchor boxes fit them poorly.
- **Reading is a sequence problem.** Context such as the neighbor letters helps decide whether a stroke is `l` or `1`.

So most OCR systems split the job: a **detector** finds word or line regions, and a **recognizer** reads each cropped region as a sequence.

blocks.title: The classic document pipeline and where errors travel

nodes.label:
OCR-free model
image straight to tokens

scenes.caption: The classic pipeline: clean the image, find text regions, read each region, then put the words in order and map them to fields.
Detection and recognition are the OCR core. The detector only says where text is; the recognizer only reads one cropped line or word at a time.
Errors propagate. If the recognizer reads `l` as `1`, or the detector misses the total, every later stage works from the wrong input and cannot recover it.
OCR-free models (lesson 5) skip the separate OCR step: one network reads the page image and writes the structured output directly.

blocks.md:
[Tesseract](https://tesseract-ocr.github.io/tessdoc/Command-Line-Usage.html) is the classic open-source engine. Since version 4.00 its main recognizer is an LSTM network that reads one text line at a time, and it keeps its own layout analysis to find lines on a page. `--oem 1` selects the LSTM engine and `--oem 0` the legacy engine (legacy models ship only in the `tessdata` repo).

The *page segmentation mode* (`--psm`) tells Tesseract what kind of image to expect. The default, 3, is fully automatic page segmentation. Mode 6 assumes a single uniform block, 7 a single text line, 8 a single word, 11 sparse text in no particular order, and 13 a raw line that bypasses Tesseract-specific hacks.

blocks.code:
# whole page, default segmentation (psm 3), LSTM engine
tesseract page.png out --oem 1

# a cropped single line, such as the total on a receipt
tesseract total_crop.png - --psm 7

# word boxes and confidences for a later layout step
tesseract page.png out hocr
tesseract page.png out tsv
blocks.caption: Command-line usage from the Tesseract manual. hOCR and TSV outputs include a bounding box per word.

blocks.md: Input quality matters as much as the model. The [Tesseract quality guide](https://tesseract-ocr.github.io/tessdoc/ImproveQuality.html) says it works best on images of at least 300 dpi, binarizes internally with Otsu's method (Tesseract 5 adds Adaptive Otsu and Sauvola), and suggests fixing rotation and skew, borders and noise before OCR. It also notes that its dictionaries are tuned for sentences, so receipts, price lists and codes may improve with dictionaries disabled or a character whitelist.

A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.
OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

blocks.question: Your app crops the 'Amount due' line from a scanned bill and calls Tesseract with default settings. It often returns an empty string even though the crop is sharp. What is the most likely first fix?
options: Retrain the LSTM model on bills
Switch to the legacy engine with --oem 0
Set the page segmentation mode to treat the image as a single line (--psm 7)
Downscale the crop so the text is smaller
blocks.explain: The default mode 3 runs full page segmentation, which expects a page of text. For a single cropped line, mode 7 tells Tesseract to skip layout analysis and read one line. Retraining or switching engines does not address the segmentation mismatch, and shrinking the text works against the 300 dpi guidance.

blocks.question: A receipt pipeline reads every character correctly, yet it reports the subtotal as the total. Which stage most likely failed?
options: Layout analysis and field mapping: the right words were read but linked to the wrong field
Text detection: the total was never found
Recognition: the digits were misread
Binarization: the image was too dark
blocks.explain: If every character was read correctly, detection and recognition did their jobs. Picking the wrong number is a structure problem, which is exactly what the layout-aware models in lesson 5 address.

lessons.title: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold

blocks.md:
From the prerequisite course you know detectors that output boxes and clean up duplicates with non-maximum suppression (NMS). Text detectors reuse those ideas but must handle words that are long, thin, rotated, or curved.

Two influential designs predict a dense map over the image instead of a small set of anchor boxes.

**EAST** ([Zhou et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.03155)) is a fully convolutional network that, at every output pixel, predicts a *score map* value in [0, 1] (is this pixel inside text?) and a *geometry*: either RBOX, 5 channels holding the distances from the pixel to the top, right, bottom and left edges of its rotated box plus the rotation angle, or QUAD, 8 channels holding offsets to the four corners.

Pixels above a score threshold each propose a box, which yields tens of thousands of candidates. EAST merges them with *locality-aware NMS*: it walks the candidates row by row and merges each with the previous one when they overlap, averaging coordinates weighted by score instead of keeping only the best. The paper reports an F-score of 0.7820 on ICDAR 2015 at 13.2 fps on 720p images.

**DBNet** ([Liao et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08947)) is *segmentation-based*: it predicts a probability map $P$ saying how likely each pixel is text, which handles curved text naturally. The hard part is turning that map into separate word regions. A fixed threshold works, but it is a step function, so the network cannot learn where the threshold should be.

DBNet adds a second head that predicts a per-pixel **threshold map** $T$ and combines them with a steep sigmoid, the *differentiable binarization*:

blocks.caption: The approximate binary map. The paper sets the amplifying factor k to 50 empirically.

scenes.caption: With k = 1 the sigmoid is nearly flat: P = 0.2 maps to 0.475 and P = 0.4 to 0.525, so text and background barely separate.
With k = 50, P = 0.2 maps to 0.0067 and P = 0.4 to 0.9933. The curve now behaves like the hard step but still has a gradient near T.
Because T is predicted per pixel, it can differ across the image. The paper shows the learned threshold map is high along text borders, where separating neighbors matters.

blocks.md:
**Labels by shrinking.** Adjacent words often touch. DBNet trains the probability map on *shrunk* polygons, so neighbors are separated by a gap. Each ground-truth polygon with area $A$ and perimeter $L$ is shrunk by an offset

$D = A(1 - r^2)/L$ with shrink ratio $r = 0.4$.

At inference the threshold branch can be dropped: binarize $P$ at a constant 0.2, take connected regions, and expand each one back by $D' = A' r'/L'$ with $r' = 1.5$, where $A'$ and $L'$ are the shrunk region's area and perimeter.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 100 x 20 pixel word box

scenes.caption: Ground truth: A = 2000, L = 240. The offset is D = 2000 x (1 - 0.16) / 240 = 7.0 px on every side.
Shrunk label: 86 x 6 px. A word that touched its neighbor now has a 7 px margin on each side, so the two blobs stay separate.
Inference expands by D' = 516 x 1.5 / 184 = 4.21 px, giving about 94.4 x 14.4 px. Simplified: corners treated as straight offsets; the box is not fully restored.

blocks.title: DBNet: training path versus inference path

scenes.caption: Training: both heads feed the differentiable binarization, and all three maps are supervised (the paper's loss weights are 1.0 for the binary map and 10 for the threshold map).
Inference: the threshold branch is removed. A constant threshold on P, connected components and one expansion step produce the polygons, which keeps post-processing cheap.

blocks.md: The paper reports that DB with a ResNet-18 backbone reaches an F-measure of 82.8 on MSRA-TD500 at 62 FPS. Production toolkits such as [PaddleOCR](https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleOCR) package this kind of segmentation-based detector together with a recognizer and layout tools.

blocks.prompt: Two words on a receipt are printed with almost no gap. If you trained DBNet on full-size (unshrunk) polygons, what would go wrong at inference?
blocks.reveal: Their probability blobs would touch, so connected-component analysis would return **one** region covering both words, and the recognizer would read them as a single token. Shrinking the labels by $D$ trains the network to leave a gap between instances, and the expansion step afterwards restores most of each word's extent.

blocks.md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

blocks.question: Why does DBNet replace the hard threshold with a sigmoid of k(P - T)?
options: It makes inference faster than a comparison
It lets gradients flow so the network can learn a per-pixel threshold map
It removes the need for the probability map
It guarantees that adjacent words never merge
blocks.explain: A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere, so a threshold inside it cannot be learned. The steep sigmoid approximates the step but stays differentiable. At inference the paper actually drops this path and uses a constant threshold on P.

blocks.question: EAST outputs a box candidate at every pixel above the score threshold. Why does it use locality-aware NMS instead of standard NMS?
options: Standard NMS cannot handle rotated boxes at all
Locality-aware NMS keeps more boxes for higher recall
Standard NMS needs anchor boxes, which EAST lacks
With tens of thousands of candidates, quadratic NMS is too slow; merging row by row is close to linear when neighbors overlap
blocks.explain: The paper notes naive NMS is O(n^2) in the number of candidates, and dense predictions give tens of thousands of them. Neighboring pixels predict nearly the same box, so merging consecutive ones in row order is fast, and weighted averaging also stabilizes the result.

lessons.title: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding

blocks.md:
Once a line or word is cropped, the recognizer must output a string of unknown length. **CRNN** ([Shi et al. 2015](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.05717)) does it in three parts:

1. **Convolutional layers** turn the image, scaled to a height of 32 pixels, into feature maps. Each *column* of the maps becomes one feature vector, so the image becomes a left-to-right sequence of *frames*, each describing a narrow vertical strip.
2. **A deep bidirectional LSTM** reads the frames and outputs, for every frame, a probability distribution over the characters plus one extra symbol, the *blank*.
3. **Transcription** turns those per-frame distributions into the final string.

With rectangular pooling, a 100 x 32 image of about 10 characters yields 25 frames, more than most English words need.

blocks.title: CRNN from pixels to a string

scenes.caption: Convolutions and pooling squeeze the height away; each column of the feature maps describes a narrow strip of the line, in left-to-right order.
The BiLSTM sees context in both directions, which helps with wide characters spanning several frames and look-alikes such as i and l.
CTC turns T per-frame distributions into a string of any length up to T, without ever being told which frame belongs to which character.

blocks.md: The training data is just (image, text) pairs. Nobody labels which frames show the `b` in `book`. **Connectionist Temporal Classification** (CTC, [Graves et al. 2006](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~graves/icml_2006.pdf)) solves this alignment problem with a many-to-one map $\mathcal{B}$ from a frame-level *path* to a label: first merge repeated symbols, then delete blanks. Graves et al. give the example $\mathcal{B}(a{-}ab{-}) = \mathcal{B}({-}aa{-}{-}abb) = aab$, where $-$ is the blank.

blocks.caption: The probability of a label sequence is the sum over every path that collapses to it. Training minimizes the negative log of this for the true label; the forward-backward algorithm computes the sum efficiently.

blocks.title: Toy recognizer output: 10 frames over {blank, b, o, k}

scenes.caption: Each column is one frame's softmax output (columns sum to 1). This is an invented toy for the word 'book', small enough to check by hand.
Greedy (best path) decoding takes the argmax in every column: b b - o o - o k k -.
Frame t6 is the interesting one: blank 0.55 versus o 0.35. That blank is the only thing separating the two o's.

blocks.title: Collapsing the best path step by step

scenes.caption: Start from the argmax symbol of each of the 10 frames.
Step 1, merge repeats: frames t2, t5 and t9 repeat the symbol just before them, so they collapse into it.
After merging: b - o - o k -. The blank at t6 stopped the two o's from merging, because they are not adjacent repeats.
Step 2, drop blanks: the output is 'book'. This path alone has probability 0.0228, the product of the 10 highlighted cells.

blocks.prompt: Suppose frame t6 had output o instead of blank, so the path is b b - o o o o k k -. What string does greedy decoding produce?
blocks.reveal: **bok**. Merging repeats turns o o o o into a single o, and nothing separates them. CTC can only spell a doubled letter if at least one blank sits between the two copies. In the original toy (t6 still mostly blank), summing over all paths already gives p(book) = 0.196 against p(bok) = 0.142, so that one frame decides a lot.

blocks.md: Notice that the best single path has probability 0.0228, yet the total probability of 'book', summed over every path that collapses to it, is 0.196. Many alignments spell the same word. Greedy decoding is cheap but Graves et al. note it is *not guaranteed* to find the most probable label; prefix search or beam search decoding approximate the sum better. CRNN also offers *lexicon-based* transcription: pick the dictionary word with the highest $p(\mathbf{l} \mid \mathbf{y})$, searching only words within a small edit distance of the greedy output using a BK-tree.

blocks.title: Greedy CTC decoding in a few lines

scenes.caption: Argmax per frame gives the path indices for b b - o o - o k k -.
Frame t2 repeats b, so it is skipped: s equals prev.
Frame t7 is o after a blank, so it is appended even though an o was emitted before. Blanks reset prev.
After the last frame the merged, blank-free string is returned.

blocks.md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.
Merging repeats happens **before** removing blanks. Doing it in the other order would turn b - o - o k into b o o k and then merge the o's into 'bok'.

blocks.question: A greedy CTC decoder sees the argmax path  - - c c - a a - t t - t  (with - as blank). What does it output?
options: cat
catt
ccaatt
catat
blocks.explain: Merge repeats first: - c - a - t - t. Then drop blanks: c a t t. The blank between the two t groups keeps them as separate characters.

blocks.question: What does a CTC-trained recognizer need as training labels for each cropped line image?
options: A bounding box around every character
The frame index where each character starts
A segmentation mask of each glyph
Only the transcript string of the line
blocks.explain: CTC sums over all alignments that collapse to the transcript, so the model learns alignment on its own. This is the property CRNN highlights: train from images and label sequences with no character-level annotation.

lessons.title: Scoring OCR output: edit distance, CER and WER

blocks.md:
To compare OCR engines you need a number. The standard tool is the **Levenshtein edit distance**: the fewest single-symbol *substitutions* (S), *deletions* (D) and *insertions* (I) that turn the reference into the prediction.

**Character error rate** (CER) counts edits over characters; **word error rate** (WER) counts them over words. Both divide by $N$, the length of the *reference*.

blocks.caption: Same formula at two granularities, as in the Hugging Face evaluate metric cards for CER and WER.

blocks.md: Worked example. Reference: `total due 125.00` (16 characters, 3 words). Prediction: `tota1 due: 12500`. Both strings happen to be 16 characters long, but that does not mean only substitutions happened.

scenes.caption: An optimal alignment from the edit-distance table. Gaps (empty cells) show where one string has a symbol and the other does not.
Substitution: l was read as 1, a classic OCR confusion.
Insertion: a colon appears in the prediction that is not in the reference.
Deletion: the decimal point was dropped. Total 3 edits over 16 reference characters: CER = 3/16 = 0.1875.

blocks.md: Now at word level. The reference words are `total`, `due`, `125.00`; the predicted words are `tota1`, `due:`, `12500`. Every word differs by at least one character, so the cheapest alignment is three substitutions.

scenes.caption: Cell (i, j) is the distance between the first i reference words and the first j predicted words. Row 0 and column 0 count pure insertions or deletions.
Each cell is the minimum of: left + 1 (insert), up + 1 (delete), diagonal + 0 if the words match, else + 1 (substitute). 'total' and 'tota1' differ, so (1,1) = 0 + 1.
Filled table. The bottom-right cell is 3: three word substitutions over 3 reference words, so WER = 1.0 while CER was only 0.1875.

blocks.prompt: If you strip punctuation from both strings before scoring (reference becomes `total due 12500`, prediction `tota1 due 12500`), what happens to CER and WER?
blocks.reveal: Only the l versus 1 substitution remains. CER drops to 1/15 = 0.067 and WER to 1/3 = 0.333. Normalization choices (case, punctuation, whitespace) can move the score more than a model change, so always report how you normalized.

scenes.caption: One wrong character spoils a whole word, so WER is much harsher than CER on short numeric fields.

blocks.md: Two details from the [Hugging Face CER metric card](https://huggingface.co/spaces/evaluate-metric/cer): $N$ is the reference length (correct plus substituted plus deleted characters), and CER is not bounded by 1, because insertions are unlimited. Reference `cat` against prediction `c a t !!` needs 5 insertions, so CER = 5/3 = 1.67.

For documents, CER tracks how well the recognizer reads glyphs, while WER (or exact match per field) tracks whether downstream code can use the result. A price with one wrong digit is a 0.17 CER on 6 characters but a 100 percent wrong field.

blocks.question: An engine outputs long runs of garbage characters on a noisy scan. A teammate says CER must still be at most 1. Are they right?
options: Yes, because CER is a ratio of edits to characters
No: insertions are counted but N is the reference length, so CER can exceed 1
Yes, because deletions are capped at N
No, because substitutions count twice
blocks.explain: CER = (S + D + I) / N with N the reference length. Every extra predicted character is an insertion, so a prediction much longer than the reference can push CER above 1.

blocks.question: You must pick one metric to decide whether an invoice-total extractor is good enough for automatic payment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Average CER over all page text
Average WER over all page text
Exact match of the normalized total field per document
Detection F-score of text boxes
blocks.explain: Payment needs the exact amount. Page-level CER can look excellent while the one field that matters has a wrong digit. Field-level exact match after agreed normalization measures what the business cares about.

lessons.title: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut

blocks.md: OCR output is a list of words with boxes. A plain text model would read them as one long sentence and lose the fact that `125.00` sits on the same row as `Total:`. **LayoutLM** ([Xu et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.13318)) keeps BERT's architecture and adds a **2D position embedding** for each word's box $(x_0, y_0, x_1, y_1)$, with $(x_0, y_0)$ the upper-left corner and $(x_1, y_1)$ the lower-right, on a page whose origin is the top-left corner.

Pages come in different sizes, so the paper scales every coordinate to a *virtual* range from 0 to 1,000. The resulting integers are **indices** into learned embedding tables: $x_0$ and $x_1$ share table X, $y_0$ and $y_1$ share table Y. The [Hugging Face LayoutLM docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/layoutlm) give the normalization as `int(1000 * x / width)` and `int(1000 * y / height)`.

blocks.title: Four OCR words on an 850 x 1100 px page

scenes.caption: Raw pixel boxes from the OCR engine (for example Tesseract's hOCR or TSV output). Values depend on scan resolution and page size.
Divide x by the width 850 and y by the height 1100, multiply by 1000 and truncate. 'Bill' becomes (70, 36, 247, 72).
'Total:' and '125.00' share y0 = 818 and y1 = 840, so they receive identical Y embeddings: the model can see they are on the same row.

blocks.tex: \mathbf{e}_i = \mathrm{Tok}(w_i) + \mathrm{Pos}(i) + X(x_0) + Y(y_0) + X(x_1) + Y(y_1) \; [\, + H(y_1 - y_0) + W(x_1 - x_0) \,]
blocks.caption: Input embedding for word i. The bracketed height and width terms are in the Hugging Face implementation (tables of size 1024 by default), not in the paper's description.

blocks.code:
def normalize_bbox(bbox, width, height):
    return [
        int(1000 * (bbox[0] / width)),
        int(1000 * (bbox[1] / height)),
        int(1000 * (bbox[2] / width)),
        int(1000 * (bbox[3] / height)),
    ]

normalize_bbox([500, 900, 572, 925], 850, 1100)
# [588, 818, 672, 840]
blocks.caption: The normalization helper from the Hugging Face LayoutLM docs, applied to the 'Total:' box.

blocks.md:
LayoutLM was pre-trained on the IIT-CDIP collection (more than 11 million scanned page images) with a *masked visual-language model* objective: mask some words but keep their 2D positions, then predict the words. Its boxes came from Tesseract. On FUNSD form understanding it raised F1 from 70.72 to 79.27.

**LayoutLMv3** ([Huang et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08387)) adds the image itself without a CNN or object detector: the page is resized to 224 x 224 and cut into 16 x 16 patches (196 patches), each linearly projected like in a vision transformer. It uses segment-level boxes (words in one text segment share a box) and pre-trains with masked language modeling, masked image modeling and a word-patch alignment objective.

**Donut** ([Kim et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.15664)) drops the OCR engine entirely. A Swin Transformer encoder reads the image (2560 x 1920 input in the paper), and a BART-style decoder generates tokens. Pre-training teaches it to *read*: output all page text in reading order, a pseudo-OCR task, on IIT-CDIP plus synthetic pages from their SynthDoG generator. Fine-tuning teaches it to *understand*: emit a token sequence such as `[START total]125.00[END total]` that converts one-to-one into JSON. If the structure is malformed, for example a START without its END, that field is treated as lost.

scenes.caption: OCR-based: an external engine produces words and boxes; LayoutLM labels each token (for example as the start of a 'total' entity), and simple code assembles fields.
OCR-free: Donut maps pixels straight to a token sequence that parses into JSON. No OCR cost or OCR error propagation, but no word boxes to show where an answer came from.

blocks.md: General vision-language models now apply the same idea at larger scale: they read the page image and answer in text. Images of pages are even used directly for retrieval, as in [ColPali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449), which embeds page images instead of extracted text.

Forgetting to normalize is a classic bug. Raw pixel coordinates from a 1700 x 2200 scan exceed the 1024-entry position tables and crash with an index error, or, if clipped, silently collapse the lower part of the page onto the same embedding.

Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

blocks.question: In LayoutLM's input, why are the coordinates scaled to integers between 0 and 1000?
options: To compress the page image
Because BERT's vocabulary has 1000 tokens
So the same position means the same relative place on any page size, and the integer can index an embedding table
To make the boxes rotation invariant
blocks.explain: The paper scales coordinates to a virtual 0 to 1,000 range because page sizes vary. The integer values are looked up in learned X and Y tables, so they must be bounded integers.

blocks.question: A team must extract fields from millions of scanned forms in a language their OCR engine handles poorly, and they do not need word-level boxes. Which approach does the Donut paper argue for?
options: An OCR-free model trained end to end, possibly pre-trained on synthetic pages in that language
LayoutLM with the existing OCR engine, since OCR errors do not matter
Tesseract with --psm 11
Rules over the OCR text
blocks.explain: Donut's motivation lists OCR cost, inflexibility of OCR across languages and document types, and OCR error propagation. Its SynthDoG generator exists precisely to pre-train in new languages and domains.

lessons.title: Judging answers on documents with ANLS

blocks.md: Document visual question answering asks a question about a page image, such as 'What is the total?'. **DocVQA** ([Mathew et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00398)) has 50,000 questions on more than 12,000 document images. Human performance on it is 94.36 percent accuracy. The authors find the answer is a substring of the serialized OCR text for more than 85 percent of questions (a stricter token subsequence for about 76 percent), so reading quality matters a lot.

Exact-match accuracy gives zero credit for `Ana Si1va` against `Ana Silva`, even though the model found the right answer and only one glyph was misread. DocVQA therefore uses **ANLS**, Average Normalized Levenshtein Similarity, introduced for scene-text VQA by [Biten et al. 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.13648). For each question take the best similarity over its ground-truth answers, and average over questions:

blocks.caption: NL is the edit distance normalized to 0 to 1 (divided by the longer string's length in common implementations). The threshold is tau = 0.5.

blocks.title: Per-answer score as a function of normalized distance

scenes.caption: Below tau the score falls off linearly with the distance. At or above tau it drops to 0: Biten et al. reason that getting more than half the answer wrong means the model picked the wrong text.
With tau = 1 there is no cliff, and a completely wrong answer of similar length could still earn partial credit. The threshold stops that.

blocks.md:
Worked example with three questions (strings compared in lowercase here):

1. Ground truth `125.00`, prediction `125.00`: distance 0, score 1.
2. Ground truths `Ana Silva` or `A. Silva`, prediction `Ana Si1va`: against `Ana Silva` the distance is 1 over 9 characters, NL = 0.111, score 0.889; against `A. Silva` NL = 3/9 = 0.333, score 0.667. Take the max: 0.889.
3. Ground truth `2024-03-05`, prediction `March 5`: distance 9 over 10 characters, NL = 0.9, which is at least 0.5, so the score is 0.

blocks.title: Exact match versus ANLS on the three answers

scenes.caption: Exact match: only Q1 counts, so accuracy = 1/3 = 0.333.
ANLS: Q2 earns 0.889 for a one-character OCR slip, Q3 still earns 0. Mean = (1 + 0.889 + 0) / 3 = 0.630.

blocks.prompt: Q3's prediction 'March 5' may be the same date as '2024-03-05'. Does ANLS give it any credit?
blocks.reveal: No. ANLS is purely string-based: NL = 0.9 is past the threshold, so the score is 0. ANLS forgives small reading errors, not paraphrases or reformatting. A generative model that rephrases or reformats an answer is penalized even when it is semantically right.

blocks.md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

blocks.question: Ground truth '42.50', prediction '42.5'. What does this answer contribute to ANLS with tau = 0.5?
options: 0, because it is not an exact match
1, because the numbers are equal
blocks.explain: One deletion over the longer length of 5 gives NL = 0.2, which is below 0.5, so the score is 1 - 0.2 = 0.8.

blocks.question: Why does ANLS include the threshold tau instead of always scoring 1 - NL?
options: To make the metric faster to compute
So that an answer that is mostly wrong text earns nothing instead of partial credit
To handle multiple ground-truth answers
To ignore case differences
blocks.explain: Biten et al. argue that an answer more than half wrong is likely the wrong text chosen from the image, not a misread of the right text. Without the cut, random strings of the right length would collect partial credit.
